tossups.p: Beta-blockers such as propranolol [“proh-PRAN-oh-lol”] slow the heart by blocking this compound’s effects. By acting on beta-2 receptors, this compound relaxes the smooth muscle wrapped around the airways, widening them so breathing is easier.
tossups.r: Auto-injectors called EpiPens deliver this drug during severe allergic reactions. For 10 points, name this hormone made by the adrenal glands.

tossups.p: Dentists often mix this compound into numbing drugs like lidocaine, since it narrows nearby blood vessels and makes the numbness last longer. In an emergency, it narrows blood vessels in the skin and gut but widens those in skeletal muscle.
tossups.r: A sudden burst of it makes your heart pound. For 10 points, name this “fight-or-flight” hormone made by the adrenal glands.

tossups.p: Physiologist Walter Cannon showed that fear and pain make the body release extra amounts of this substance into the blood. It raises blood sugar by making the liver break down glycogen, a process called glycogenolysis [“gly-koh-jeh-NOL-ih-sis”].
tossups.r: Cannon named the response it drives “fight or flight.” For 10 points, name this hormone made by the adrenal glands.

tossups.p: Cells build this compound from the amino acid tyrosine in four steps, passing through L-DOPA and dopamine along the way. Its structure includes a catechol group, a benzene ring carrying two hydroxyl groups.
tossups.r: Its close relative norepinephrine differs from it by just one methyl group. For 10 points, name this “fight-or-flight” hormone.

tossups.p: This hormone binds beta-1 receptors in the heart to make it beat faster and harder, and it binds alpha-1 receptors on blood vessels to narrow them and raise blood pressure. In the liver, it switches on the breakdown of glycogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone released by the adrenal glands during the “fight-or-flight” response.

tossups.p: Emergency teams give repeated doses of this drug during CPR for cardiac arrest, to help get the heart beating again. Within the body, this compound widens the pupils and the airways when danger appears.
tossups.r: It is the drug inside EpiPens. For 10 points, name this hormone that the adrenal glands release in the “fight-or-flight” response.

tossups.p: American pharmacologist John Jacob Abel gave this hormone its Greek-based name, which means “on the kidney.” Its Latin-based name means nearly the same thing and is the one more often used in Britain.
tossups.r: People describe feeling a “rush” of it when they are scared. For 10 points, name this “fight-or-flight” hormone.

tossups.p: The cells that make this compound develop from the neural crest, the same embryo tissue that forms many nerve cells, so the tissue holding them works like a modified sympathetic ganglion.
tossups.r: That tissue, the adrenal medulla, releases this hormone during stress. For 10 points, name this “fight-or-flight” hormone that EpiPens inject.

tossups.p: Doctors inject this drug into the muscle of the outer thigh as the first treatment for anaphylaxis [“an-uh-fuh-LAK-sis”], a severe allergic reaction that can swell the throat and drop blood pressure. It works with the sympathetic nervous system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone, made by the adrenal glands, that triggers the “fight-or-flight” response.

tossups.p: This hormone widens the pupils by tightening the spoke-like dilator muscle of each iris, and it slows down digestion. It also makes fat cells break down stored fat for fuel.
tossups.r: Its release makes the heart race. For 10 points, name this “fight-or-flight” hormone made by the adrenal glands, the drug in EpiPens.

clues.t: The main hormone of the “fight-or-flight” response to danger or stress
Made mainly by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys
The drug in EpiPens, auto-injectors that treat anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction
A sudden “rush” of it makes the heart pound, the airways open, and the pupils widen
Released by the adrenal medulla, the inner part of each adrenal gland; the outer cortex makes cortisol instead
Works hand in hand with the sympathetic nervous system, which revs the body up for action
A catecholamine, like dopamine and norepinephrine; built from the amino acid tyrosine by way of L-DOPA and dopamine
Its close relative norepinephrine (noradrenaline) differs from it by just one methyl group
Raises blood sugar by making the liver break down glycogen (glycogenolysis); also makes fat cells release fat
Its two names mean “on the kidney” (Greek) and “near the kidneys” (Latin); the Latin one is more common in Britain
Given in repeated doses during CPR for cardiac arrest
Widens the airways through beta-2 receptors; beta-blockers such as propranolol block its effects on the heart
Earl Sutherland won a Nobel Prize (1971) after finding the “second messenger” cyclic AMP while studying how it breaks down liver glycogen
Japanese chemist Jokichi Takamine isolated it in 1901; he also helped arrange Japan’s 1912 gift of cherry trees to Washington, D.C.
American pharmacologist John Jacob Abel gave it its Greek-based name
The enzyme PNMT makes it by adding a methyl group to norepinephrine; cortisol boosts that enzyme
Chromaffin cells store it in granules and release it when sympathetic nerves signal them with acetylcholine
Its source cells come from the neural crest, so the adrenal medulla works like a modified sympathetic ganglion
A rare tumor called pheochromocytoma can release too much of it, causing headaches, sweating, and a pounding heartbeat
Broken down after release by the enzymes MAO and COMT; its catechol group is a benzene ring with two hydroxyl groups
Mixed into numbing drugs like lidocaine to narrow nearby blood vessels so the numbness lasts longer
Physiologist Walter Cannon showed that fear and pain increase its release, and named the “fight or flight” response
Narrows blood vessels in the skin and gut but widens those in skeletal muscle
Binds alpha and beta receptors: beta-1 makes the heart beat faster and harder, alpha-1 narrows blood vessels
For anaphylaxis, it is injected into the muscle of the outer thigh as the first treatment

trap.title: Epinephrine or norepinephrine?
trap.body: Norepinephrine (also called noradrenaline) is this hormone’s near-twin: both are catecholamines, both come from the adrenal medulla, and both power the “fight-or-flight” response. Answering the wrong twin loses the tossup. Players also blurt “adrenal glands,” which names the organ rather than the chemical, or “cortisol,” the stress hormone from the gland’s outer layer.
trap.fix: Norepinephrine is mainly the messenger released by sympathetic nerve endings and by brain cells in the locus coeruleus, so listen for those. EpiPens, anaphylaxis, PNMT, and Takamine mean epinephrine (or adrenaline). If the question asks for “this gland,” say adrenal glands.
trap.line: Real answer line: Epinephrine (accept adrenaline or adrenalin; prompt on catecholamine; do not accept “norepinephrine” or “noradrenaline”)

topics.name: ATP
topics.kicker: Adenosine triphosphate · The energy currency of every living cell
topics.briefing: ATP, short for adenosine triphosphate, is the energy “money” that every living cell spends. Its three phosphate groups are crammed tightly together, and snapping off the last one releases energy that powers muscles, pumps, and nearly every other job in the cell. Your cells keep rebuilding it from the leftover ADP, mostly inside their mitochondria.
topics.answerHtml: ATP (accept adenosine triphosphate; do not accept “ADP,” “AMP,” or “ATP synthase”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Paul Boyer and John Walker shared a Nobel Prize for explaining how a spinning enzyme assembles this molecule as hydrogen ions flow through it. Peter Mitchell’s chemiosmotic theory had earlier explained where that flow of ions comes from.
tossups.r: Mitochondria make most of this molecule. For 10 points, name this “energy currency” of the cell.

tossups.p: Fritz Lipmann marked the “high-energy” phosphate bonds in this molecule with a squiggle, years after Karl Lohmann discovered it in 1929. Alexander Todd first made this molecule in a laboratory in 1948.
tossups.r: Breaking off its last phosphate group leaves ADP. For 10 points, name this energy-carrying molecule that powers most of a cell’s work.

tossups.p: Fireflies glow when the enzyme luciferase uses this molecule to power a reaction with luciferin, so scientists use firefly enzymes to measure how much of this molecule a sample holds. Enzymes called kinases move one of its phosphate groups onto other molecules.
tossups.r: Cellular respiration makes it. For 10 points, name this “energy currency” of cells, made mostly in the mitochondria.

tossups.p: Each cycle of the sodium-potassium pump spends one of these molecules to push three sodium ions out of a cell and bring two potassium ions in. Active transport like that needs this molecule because it moves substances against their concentration gradient.
tossups.r: Cells rebuild it from ADP. For 10 points, name this energy molecule made of adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups.

tossups.p: Myosin heads in muscle need a fresh one of these molecules to let go of actin, so when the body runs out of them after death, muscles lock stiff in rigor mortis. Creatine phosphate quickly rebuilds these molecules during a sprint.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this molecule that releases energy when it loses a phosphate group and becomes ADP.

tossups.p: In cyclic photophosphorylation, electrons loop back through photosystem I, so a chloroplast makes only this molecule and no NADPH. The light reactions of photosynthesis normally make this molecule and NADPH to power the Calvin cycle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this molecule that stores energy in the bonds between its three phosphate groups.

tossups.p: High levels of this molecule slow down glycolysis by blocking the enzyme phosphofructokinase, a classic example of feedback inhibition. Hexokinase spends one of these molecules in glycolysis’s first step to attach a phosphate group to glucose.
tossups.r: Glycolysis still ends with a net gain of two of them. For 10 points, name this energy molecule, the cell’s “energy currency.”

tossups.p: Breaking the bond to this molecule’s gamma phosphate, the one farthest from its sugar, releases about 7.3 kilocalories per mole under standard conditions. That reaction is a hydrolysis, because a water molecule is used to split off the phosphate.
tossups.r: The molecule left behind is ADP. For 10 points, name this “energy currency” of the cell.

tossups.p: Protons flow through a membrane-spanning rotor that spins a central stalk inside a knob-shaped head, and each full turn of that stalk builds three of these molecules. That machine sits in the inner membrane of mitochondria and in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy-storing molecule, which the machine makes by adding a phosphate to ADP.

tossups.p: The enzyme adenylyl cyclase [“uh-DEN-uh-lil SYE-klayss”] turns this molecule into cyclic AMP, a common signal inside cells. RNA polymerase uses this molecule as one of its four building blocks when it builds a strand of RNA.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nucleotide that carries energy in its three phosphate groups, the cell’s main energy source.

tossups.p: Inside cells, this molecule is usually bound to a magnesium ion, which most enzymes need in order to use it. When it loses two phosphates at once instead of one, it releases pyrophosphate and becomes AMP.
tossups.r: Cellular respiration in the mitochondria makes most of it. For 10 points, name this molecule that powers most of a cell’s work.

tossups.p: The Krebs cycle makes only a little of this molecule directly, but it supplies NADH and FADH2 to the electron transport chain, which drives oxidative phosphorylation to make much more. Textbooks estimate that fully breaking down one glucose molecule yields about 30 to 38 of these molecules.
tossups.r: Mitochondria make most of it. For 10 points, name this “energy currency” molecule that becomes ADP when it is used.

tossups.p: Two phosphoanhydride [“FOSS-foh-an-HY-dride”] bonds link this molecule’s three phosphate groups, which are labeled alpha, beta, and gamma. Its five-carbon sugar is ribose, and its base is adenine, a purine, so this molecule is a nucleotide.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this molecule that becomes ADP when it gives up energy, the cell’s “energy currency.”

tossups.p: Cells drive uphill, energy-absorbing endergonic [“en-der-GON-ik”] reactions by coupling them to the breakdown of this molecule, which releases energy. That breakdown also powers motor proteins like kinesin and dynein that carry cargo along microtubules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this molecule, the main “energy currency” of cells, which becomes ADP when it is used.

tossups.p: Fermentation lets yeast and muscle cells keep making small amounts of this molecule without oxygen by recycling NAD+. When oxygen is present, mitochondria can make many more of these molecules from each sugar molecule.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy-carrying molecule that has three phosphate groups and becomes ADP when it is used.

clues.t: The cell’s main “energy currency,” powering most of its work
Made of the base adenine, the sugar ribose, and three phosphate groups
Releases energy when it loses its last phosphate group, leaving ADP, which has only two
Mitochondria, the “powerhouse of the cell,” make most of it
Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to make it
Glycolysis makes a net gain of two for each glucose; fermentation lets cells keep making those two without oxygen
Most of it comes from oxidative phosphorylation, powered by the electron transport chain; one glucose yields about 30 to 38 in all
Hydrogen ions flowing back across a membrane (chemiosmosis) power the spinning enzyme that builds it from ADP
The light reactions of photosynthesis make it, along with NADPH, to power the Calvin cycle
Powers active transport: the sodium-potassium pump spends one to move 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in
Hydrolysis (splitting with water) of the bond to its last phosphate releases energy
Muscles use it to make myosin pull on actin and then let go
A nucleotide; RNA polymerase uses it as one of its four building blocks for RNA
Paul Boyer and John Walker shared a 1997 Nobel Prize for explaining the spinning enzyme that makes it
Peter Mitchell’s chemiosmotic theory explained how a flow of ions powers its production
Protons turn the enzyme’s membrane rotor, spinning a stalk inside a knob-shaped head; each full turn builds three
Karl Lohmann discovered it in 1929; Fritz Lipmann marked its “high-energy” bonds with a squiggle; Alexander Todd first synthesized it in 1948
The firefly enzyme luciferase uses it to make luciferin glow, so scientists use that glow to measure it
Enzymes called kinases move one of its phosphate groups onto other molecules (phosphorylation); hexokinase does this to glucose
High levels of it block the enzyme phosphofructokinase, slowing glycolysis (feedback inhibition)
Its phosphates are named alpha, beta, and gamma, joined by phosphoanhydride bonds; losing the gamma phosphate releases about 7.3 kcal per mole
Without it, myosin can’t let go of actin, causing rigor mortis; creatine phosphate quickly rebuilds it in sprinting muscles
The enzyme adenylyl cyclase turns it into the signal molecule cyclic AMP
Usually bound to a magnesium ion in cells; losing two phosphates at once releases pyrophosphate and leaves AMP
Cyclic photophosphorylation, with electrons looping through photosystem I, makes it without making NADPH
Energy coupling: its breakdown drives uphill endergonic reactions and motor proteins like kinesin and dynein

trap.title: ATP, ADP, or the enzyme?
trap.body: ADP (adenosine diphosphate) is what is left after ATP spends a phosphate, and AMP has only one phosphate, so naming the wrong one loses the tossup. Many questions also describe the spinning enzyme that builds ATP. If the question asks for “this enzyme,” the answer is ATP synthase, not the molecule, and “this organelle” means mitochondria.
trap.fix: Count the phosphates: “tri” means three, “di” means two. Listen to the noun: “this molecule” or “this nucleotide” that carries energy means ATP; “this enzyme” or “this rotary motor” means ATP synthase.
trap.line: Real answer line: ATP (accept adenosine triphosphate; do not accept “ADP,” “AMP,” or “ATP synthase”)

topics.name: Birds
topics.kicker: Feathered, egg-laying vertebrates · The only dinosaurs still alive
topics.briefing: Birds are the only animals alive today with feathers, and scientists consider them living dinosaurs, descended from the same branch of dinosaurs as Tyrannosaurus rex. Hollow bones, big flight muscles, and super-efficient lungs let most of them fly, from the tiny bee hummingbird of Cuba to the soaring albatross. The ostrich can’t fly at all, but it lays the biggest eggs of any living bird.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: These animals make sounds with a syrinx [“SIR-inks”], a vocal organ found where the windpipe splits toward the two lungs. Many of them grind their food in a muscular stomach called a gizzard, often with the help of swallowed stones.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of animals, the only living animals that have feathers.

tossups.p: Air sacs let these animals move air through their lungs in only one direction, so fresh air flows past gas-exchange tubes called parabronchi both when they breathe in and when they breathe out.
tossups.r: Many of their bones are hollow and filled with air. For 10 points, name these feathered, egg-laying animals, which include robins and eagles.

tossups.p: Flightless ratites [“RAT-ites”] such as emus and kiwis lack the keel, a ridge on the breastbone that anchors the big flight muscles of most of these animals. Most other members have fused collarbones forming a springy furcula [“FUR-kyoo-luh”], better known as the wishbone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of feathered animals that includes ostriches, penguins, and eagles.

tossups.p: In 1861, a feathered fossil called Archaeopteryx [“ar-kee-OP-ter-iks”] was found in the Solnhofen [“ZOHLN-hoh-fen”] limestone of Germany, and Thomas Henry Huxley later argued that these animals evolved from dinosaurs. Scientists now place them among the theropods, the same group as Tyrannosaurus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these animals with feathers and beaks, often called the only living dinosaurs.

tossups.p: John James Audubon’s giant book about these animals, published in parts from 1827 to 1838, reproduced his paintings in 435 life-size, hand-colored plates. The branch of science that studies these animals is called ornithology.
tossups.r: Examples include robins, eagles, owls, and penguins. For 10 points, name this class of feathered, egg-laying animals that descended from dinosaurs.

tossups.p: Peter and Rosemary Grant spent decades on the Galápagos island of Daphne Major, measuring how droughts changed the beaks of some of these animals. Charles Darwin had collected those animals, now called Darwin’s finches, whose beak shapes fit different foods.
tossups.r: They have beaks but no teeth. For 10 points, name this class of feathered, egg-laying animals.

tossups.p: Konrad Lorenz showed that newly hatched goslings would follow him as if he were their mother, a kind of learning called imprinting. Chicks of these animals that hatch helpless and naked are called altricial, while those that can walk and feed right away are precocial.
tossups.r: Ducks and geese belong to this class. For 10 points, name these egg-laying animals with feathers.

tossups.p: These animals conserve water by getting rid of nitrogen waste as a white paste of uric acid, which leaves the body through a single opening called the cloaca [“kloh-AY-kuh”]. Their eggs have hard shells made of calcium carbonate.
tossups.r: Their front limbs are wings. For 10 points, name these warm-blooded animals that have feathers and beaks.

tossups.p: Tiny hooks on barbules [“BAR-byoolz”] zip together the barbs of these animals’ most distinctive body coverings, and a gland near the tail makes the oil these animals spread while preening. They replace those coverings in a process called molting.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these animals, the only living creatures covered in feathers, which include eagles and owls.

tossups.p: The last few tail vertebrae of these animals are fused into a pygostyle [“PYE-guh-style”], which supports their tail feathers, and many of their lower-back vertebrae are fused into a synsacrum [“sin-SAY-krum”] that is joined to the hips. Their bones are often hollow, with thin inner struts for strength.
tossups.r: Most of them can fly. For 10 points, name this class of feathered vertebrates that lay hard-shelled eggs.

tossups.p: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, and the flightless dodo of Mauritius [“maw-RISH-us”] had vanished by the late 1600s, less than a century after Dutch sailors first landed there. Both belonged to this class of animals.
tossups.r: Living members include pigeons, parrots, and penguins. For 10 points, name this class of feathered animals.

tossups.p: Some of these animals, such as cuckoos, are brood parasites that lay their eggs in other species’ nests, so the hosts raise their chicks. The Arctic tern, one of these animals, makes the longest yearly migration of any animal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these feathered animals, many of which fly south for the winter.

tossups.p: Feathered fossils of Sinosauropteryx [“sye-noh-sor-OP-ter-iks”] and the four-winged Microraptor show that many dinosaurs closely related to these animals had feathers too. These animals were the only dinosaurs to survive the asteroid impact 66 million years ago.
tossups.r: Their front limbs are wings, and they have beaks but no teeth. For 10 points, name these living animals with feathers.

tossups.p: Crocodiles and alligators are the closest living relatives of these animals, and both groups are archosaurs [“AR-kuh-sorz”]. Like mammals, these animals have a four-chambered heart and are warm-blooded, though the two groups evolved those traits separately.
tossups.r: They lay hard-shelled eggs and have toothless beaks. For 10 points, name these feathered animals, which include eagles and penguins.

tossups.p: More than half of all species in this class are passerines [“PASS-uh-rynz”], a group with feet built for perching, and many passerines learn their songs from adults. Many members of this class store food in a pouch called a crop before it reaches the gizzard.
tossups.r: The largest living member is the ostrich. For 10 points, name this class of feathered animals.

Many of their bones are hollow and filled with air, which keeps them light
Archaeopteryx, a feathered fossil found in Germany in 1861, is a famous link between them and dinosaurs

trap.title: Dinosaurs, reptiles, or birds?
trap.body: Many tossups on this answer lead with dinosaur clues such as Archaeopteryx, Microraptor, and theropods, so players blurt “dinosaurs,” which is too general and earns only a prompt at best. Others hear “lay eggs,” “cloaca,” or “crocodiles” and say “reptiles.” Pterosaurs were flying reptiles, not birds and not dinosaurs.
trap.fix: Hold on for feathers, beaks, the syrinx, the gizzard, or the keel, and if a prompt comes, say birds (or Aves). Aristophanes’s comedy _The Birds_ is a separate literature answer, so listen for “this play” before answering it.
trap.line: Real answer line: Birds (accept Aves or avians; prompt on dinosaurs)

topics.name: Chloroplasts
topics.kicker: Green organelles in plant and algae cells · Where photosynthesis happens
topics.dates: Found in the cells of plants and algae
topics.briefing: Chloroplasts are the tiny green solar factories inside plant and algae cells. Packed with the pigment chlorophyll, they capture sunlight and use it to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing the oxygen we breathe. Long ago their ancestors were free-living cyanobacteria that got swallowed by a bigger cell, which is why chloroplasts still carry their own DNA.
topics.answerHtml: Chloroplasts (accept chloroplast; prompt on plastids; do not accept “chlorophyll” or “chromoplasts”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The sea slug Elysia chlorotica steals these organelles from the algae it eats and keeps them working inside its own cells for months, a trick called kleptoplasty. Each of these organelles holds stacks of flattened sacs called grana.
tossups.r: Inside them, chlorophyll captures sunlight for photosynthesis. For 10 points, name these green organelles found in plant cells.

tossups.p: In 1909, Carl Correns found that the green and white patches on variegated four o’clock plants are passed down only through the mother, because these organelles travel in the egg rather than in pollen. These organelles carry their own small, circular DNA.
tossups.r: They contain chlorophyll. For 10 points, name these organelles in which plants carry out photosynthesis.

tossups.p: Theodor Engelmann shone a prism’s rainbow onto a strand of algae and found that oxygen-loving bacteria crowded around the parts lit by red and blue light, where these organelles were working hardest. These organelles hold the pigments chlorophyll a and b along with orange carotenoids.
tossups.r: Their stacked thylakoids capture light energy. For 10 points, name these green organelles where photosynthesis takes place.

tossups.p: The alga Spirogyra [“spy-roh-JY-ruh”] is named for its ribbon-like spiral of this organelle, while Chlamydomonas [“klam-ih-doh-MOH-nus”] has one cup-shaped example holding a pyrenoid wrapped in starch. Under a microscope, these organelles drift around Elodea leaf cells by cytoplasmic streaming.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these green organelles that carry out photosynthesis in plant and algae cells.

tossups.p: Lynn Margulis championed the idea that these organelles descend from cyanobacteria that were swallowed by an ancient cell and never digested. Like mitochondria, these organelles are wrapped in two membranes and have their own circular DNA and bacteria-like ribosomes.
tossups.r: They contain the green pigment chlorophyll. For 10 points, name these organelles where plants make sugar using sunlight.

tossups.p: Some algae picked up these organelles secondhand by swallowing other algae, so their versions are wrapped in three or four membranes, and cryptophytes even keep a shrunken leftover nucleus called a nucleomorph. The malaria parasite carries a non-green relative of these organelles called the apicoplast.
tossups.r: In land plants, these organelles have just two membranes. For 10 points, name these green organelles that contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

tossups.p: These organelles divide by pinching in two with the help of FtsZ, a ring-forming protein inherited from their bacterial ancestors. Most of their proteins are made out in the cytoplasm and must be imported through gateways called TOC and TIC.
tossups.r: Their thylakoid membranes capture light energy. For 10 points, name these green organelles in plant cells.

tossups.p: The gene rbcL, which plant scientists use as a DNA barcode to tell species apart, sits in the DNA of these organelles and codes for the large subunit of RuBisCO [“roo-BIS-koh”]. That enzyme fixes carbon dioxide in the fluid called stroma inside these organelles.
tossups.r: Chlorophyll in their thylakoids absorbs light. For 10 points, name these organelles where the Calvin cycle takes place.

tossups.p: Like chromoplasts, which help turn ripe tomatoes red, and starch-storing amyloplasts, these organelles develop from small, unspecialized proplastids. Plants grown in total darkness form pale etioplasts that turn into these organelles once light arrives.
tossups.r: These green organelles hold chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. For 10 points, name this kind of plastid found in leaf cells.

tossups.p: During the light reactions, protons pile up inside the thylakoid lumen of these organelles and then rush back out into the stroma through ATP synthase. Water molecules are split inside these organelles, releasing the oxygen that plants give off.
tossups.r: Their stroma hosts the Calvin cycle. For 10 points, name these green organelles where photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: In very bright light, these organelles line up along the side walls of leaf cells to avoid damage, but in dim light they spread out across the cell to catch as much light as possible. The palisade cells of a leaf are packed with them.
tossups.r: They give leaves their green color. For 10 points, name these organelles in plant cells that contain chlorophyll.

tossups.p: Coin-like sacs called thylakoids are stacked inside this organelle into grana [“GRAY-nuh”], which are joined by flat bridges called stroma lamellae [“luh-MEL-ee”]. The thick fluid around those stacks, the stroma, is where carbon dioxide is turned into sugar.
tossups.r: Its green pigment is chlorophyll. For 10 points, name this organelle that carries out photosynthesis in plant cells.

tossups.p: In C4 plants such as corn, the Calvin cycle runs inside these organelles in bundle-sheath cells wrapped around the leaf veins. On the leaf’s outer skin, the guard cells that open and close each stoma also contain these organelles.
tossups.r: They contain the pigment chlorophyll. For 10 points, name these green organelles where photosynthesis takes place.

tossups.p: In glaucophyte [“GLAW-koh-fyte”] algae, these organelles still keep a thin layer of peptidoglycan [“pep-tih-doh-GLY-kan”], the same material found in bacterial cell walls, a clue to where they came from. Their name comes from Greek words meaning “green” and “formed.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organelles in plant and algae cells that turn light energy into chemical energy.

tossups.p: In autumn, many trees break down the chlorophyll inside these organelles, letting yellow and orange carotenoids show through. During the day, these organelles store some of the sugar they make as grains of starch.
tossups.r: Their thylakoid membranes capture sunlight. For 10 points, name these green organelles that carry out photosynthesis in plant cells.

clues.t: The organelles where photosynthesis takes place in plants and algae
Green because they hold the pigment chlorophyll; their name comes from Greek for “green” and “formed”
Found in plant and algae cells, but not in animal cells
Capture sunlight to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, giving off oxygen
Inside are coin-like sacs called thylakoids, stacked into grana and linked by stroma lamellae
The fluid around the stacks is the stroma, where the Calvin cycle turns carbon dioxide into sugar
The light reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes, splitting water and releasing oxygen
Like mitochondria, they have two membranes, their own circular DNA, and bacteria-like ribosomes
Endosymbiotic theory: they descend from cyanobacteria swallowed by an ancient cell; Lynn Margulis championed the idea
A type of plastid; relatives include chromoplasts (which color fruits) and amyloplasts (which store starch)
Packed into a leaf’s palisade cells, and found in the guard cells that open and close each stoma
Seen drifting by cytoplasmic streaming in Elodea leaf cells under a microscope
In autumn their chlorophyll breaks down, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids; they store some sugar as starch grains
The sea slug Elysia chlorotica steals them from algae it eats and keeps them working, a trick called kleptoplasty
Carl Correns (1909) showed that leaf patches on variegated four o’clocks come only from the mother, since these travel in the egg
Theodor Engelmann used a prism and oxygen-loving bacteria to show that algae work hardest in red and blue light
Spirogyra has a spiral, ribbon-like one; Chlamydomonas has a single cup-shaped one with a starchy pyrenoid
Algae that got them secondhand have versions with three or four membranes; cryptophytes keep a leftover nucleus called a nucleomorph
The malaria parasite carries a non-green relative called the apicoplast
Divide by pinching in two with the ring-forming protein FtsZ, inherited from their bacterial ancestors
Most of their proteins are made in the cytoplasm and imported through gateways called TOC and TIC
Their gene rbcL codes for the large subunit of RuBisCO and is used as a DNA barcode for plants
Develop from proplastids; plants grown in darkness form pale etioplasts that turn green in light
Protons pile up in the thylakoid lumen and rush back into the stroma through ATP synthase
In bright light they line up along cell side walls to avoid damage; in dim light they spread out
In C4 plants such as corn, the Calvin cycle runs in the ones inside bundle-sheath cells
Glaucophyte algae versions still keep a peptidoglycan layer, like a bacterial cell wall

trap.title: Chloroplast or chlorophyll?
trap.body: Chlorophyll is the green pigment; chloroplasts are the organelles that hold it. The two words look almost alike, so a fast buzz on “green” or “captures light” can come out wrong. Thylakoids and the stroma are parts of the organelle, and mitochondria are its look-alike cousin, since both have two membranes and their own DNA.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This organelle” or “this plastid” means chloroplast; “this pigment” or “this molecule” with a magnesium ion at its center means chlorophyll; “these stacked sacs” means thylakoids. Breaking down sugar for energy means mitochondria instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chloroplasts (accept chloroplast; prompt on plastids; do not accept “chlorophyll” or “chromoplasts”)
